assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, turn laser-cooled atoms into the most precise measuring instruments yet made, now at the 1e-18 level. From my own field's viewpoint this is the kind of precision that tests fundamental physics (constancy of constants, relativistic redshift across millimetres) and it rests on a clean, easily explained idea.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the strontium clock. Ye's group pushed it to record accuracy and stability and to clock comparisons. Both are named in the credit list and form a natural pair. Others (for example Lemonde, Derevianko on the theory side) may have claims that I cannot assess from the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories have reproduced and extended the clocks, with international comparisons. The field is mature, stable and still advancing. Recognition looks timely, and later redefinition of the second would reinforce it.
uncertainties: Whether a prize here is judged to overlap with the 2005 and 2012 recognition of laser spectroscopy and atom control.
Allocation of credit between the lattice-clock concept and the ultra-precise implementations, including theory contributions that are not in the credited list.
I am recalling these facts from memory and have not verified them independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices gave a clean realisation of Hubbard-type many-body models. The Mott-insulator transition, single-site-resolved microscopy and quantum simulation of strongly correlated systems let us watch quantum many-body physics directly, which links to the question of how collective behaviour emerges from quantum mechanics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and collaborators) provided the theoretical proposal. Greiner and Bloch performed the decisive Mott-insulator experiment and developed quantum-gas microscopy. Cirac is credited as well and is a strong theorist, so a three-person limit forces a difficult choice. I consider the Zoller, Bloch and Greiner combination to reflect proposal plus experiment most closely, but it is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many groups worldwide, with a mature toolbox. Quantitative agreement between theory and experiment is a strength, but the main aim of quantum simulation (solving problems beyond classical computers) is still developing.
uncertainties: Choice between Cirac, Zoller and the experimental pioneers inside a three-laureate limit.
Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize for quantum control of single particles.
Whether the practical impact of quantum simulation is already large enough for recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED realises strong light-matter coupling with artificial atoms in superconducting circuits. It is a controlled laboratory for cavity QED, with dispersive readout and the transmon as the basis of superconducting quantum processors. The physics is clear and the impact on quantum optics and quantum technology is large.
assessment.attribution: Blais, with collaborators, wrote the theoretical proposal. Wallraff and Schoelkopf with colleagues carried out the first strong-coupling experiments. The credit trio maps well onto proposal plus experiment. The transmon (Koch, Schoelkopf and others) and the contribution of Yale colleagues may be separate matters that complicate the allocation.
assessment.maturity: Many laboratories and companies reproduce the work and build on it. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so the field has just been honoured, which may make an immediate follow-up less likely, though it is a different discovery.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
Distinct credit among cavity QED proposal, first experiments and the transmon qubit.
Facts are from my memory and not independently checked.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that quantum phases carry geometric and topological content. This is a conceptual discovery that surprised physicists and now underlies much of modern physics, from molecular and atomic physics to topological matter. It is the sort of fundamental surprise I value.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov (with Bohm, who is deceased, and with Anandan in related work) and Berry are the natural pair. The credited names do not include Bohm or Pancharatnam, so the credit is incomplete as a historical account, and one needs to be careful about which discovery is actually being honoured.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed experimentally many times and used widely over decades. Any prize would be late rather than premature. The question is whether a conceptual prize can be assigned to a set of living people cleanly.
uncertainties: Aharonov-Bohm credit involves a deceased co-discoverer and earlier work by Ehrenberg and Siday.
Berry phase had precursors such as Pancharatnam.
Whether the committee would treat the topic as one discovery or two.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators opened a new class of matter characterised by topology rather than symmetry breaking. Theory predicted it (Kane and Mele, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for HgTe), and the transport experiment on HgTe wells confirmed it. This is a strong fundamental discovery with wide influence, though outside my own specialty, so I defer to colleagues on condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the original Z2 theoretical proposal. Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells. Zhang's work (the HgTe proposal) is a significant omission and Zhang is deceased. This three-person set is reasonably coherent.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by several experiments and by the development of three-dimensional topological insulators. The interpretation is stable and the field is mature, so the recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Credit among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele three-dimensional work and the experimental groups.
Overlap with the 2016 Nobel Prize for topological phases.
My own expertise in this area is limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases with tunable interactions allowed a direct study of the BEC-BCS crossover, unitary gases and universal behaviour. This is a clean, fundamental quantum many-body system whose results connect to superconductivity and nuclear matter, and the cold-atom experiments agree well with theory.
assessment.attribution: Experimental groups share the credit (condensation of fermion pairs, vortices, thermodynamics, and the universal equation of state). Four names are credited and only three can be chosen. Jin, who made a key contribution to the first fermionic condensate, is deceased and absent from the list, and there are theoretical contributors too. Allocation looks hard.
assessment.maturity: Results were reproduced by several independent laboratories and the field is mature. The interpretation is stable. Recognition is plausible, but the discovery is more incremental than a single decisive discovery.
uncertainties: Missing credit for Deborah Jin, who died in 2016.
Difficulty choosing three of four experimentalists and overlooking theory.
Whether the field is judged as one discovery or a series of advances.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum control of mechanical motion (ground-state cooling, quantum states of macroscopic oscillators, and entanglement with light) addresses directly the question of how far quantum mechanics reaches into the macroscopic world. I find that question deeply interesting, since it is the border between the quantum and ordinary worlds.
assessment.attribution: Cleland demonstrated a mechanical resonator in the quantum ground state with a superconducting qubit, Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed cavity optomechanics and its quantum regime. Teufel, Painter, Schwab and others also contributed, so a three-person list leaves out several decisive contributors.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by several groups, but the field is still young. The interpretation is stable. A prize may be somewhat early, and several recent prizes touched on related quantum control topics.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse across many groups with parallel results.
Possible premature recognition relative to older fields.
Overlap with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical discovery that in two dimensions particles can have fractional statistics (anyons) is a genuinely new and unexpected idea about how nature works. It has connected to the fractional quantum Hall effect and to proposals for topological quantum computing.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim published the 1977 statistics argument, and Wilczek coined 'anyon' and developed it in 1982. Credit seems reasonably clear and all three are named, though Wilczek is already a laureate (2004), which is a policy question for the committee.
assessment.maturity: Experimental evidence for anyonic statistics in quantum Hall interferometers and collision experiments has appeared recently (2020 onwards) and is still being scrutinised. Theory is well established, but experimental confirmation is recent, so maturity is moderate.
uncertainties: Whether recent anyon braiding experiments are independently reproduced and conclusive.
A prior laureate among the credited names.
Priority questions in the earlier literature.
